behaviours.comparison: Scope limited to serious incidents (thermal runaway, fire, explosion, injury) omits smoke and overheating events; answer key requires all thermal incidents and rates this as weakened.
behaviours.excerpt: Manufacturers must report any thermal runaway, fire, explosion, or injury involving a home battery to the relevant regulator within 72 hours of becoming aware of it.

fact_claims.verbatim: Halcyon’s company-wide rate was 8.1 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units last year
Northwind’s company-wide thermal incident rate was 8.6 per 100,000 installed units last year
Halcyon had four thermal incidents last year that were not reported to a regulator.

S1_incident_reporting.quote: Manufacturers must report any thermal runaway, fire, explosion, or injury involving a home battery to the relevant regulator within 72 hours of becoming aware of it. They must notify affected customers within 5 calendar days, including known hazards, immediate precautions, and how to obtain support. A manufacturer must provide a complete incident record to the regulator within 30 days, including cases initially reported by customers or third parties.

S2_thermal_testing.quote: Each model must undergo a sustained-heat test at 55 °C before market placement and after a material design or manufacturing change, using a regulator-approved protocol and statistically adequate sample. Results and corrective-action plans must be submitted confidentially to the relevant regulator and provided to customers who buy that model, on request and before purchase. A failure rate above 5% triggers regulator review and a documented corrective-action plan; it does not by itself prohibit market placement.

S3_remote_shutoff.quote: All new home battery units placed on the market from 3 years after this standard takes effect must support remote emergency shut-off, with safeguards against unauthorized activation and clear customer guidance. Manufacturers must provide a retrofit plan for installed units and complete retrofits, where technically feasible, within 6 years after the effective date. Customers must be informed of any unit that cannot be retrofitted and of available safety measures.

S4_fire_suppression.quote: New home battery units placed on the market from 36 months after adoption of this standard must include built-in fire suppression designed and tested to contain or limit battery fires without creating additional hazards. ... The regulator may approve an equivalent protective design where it provides comparable fire-risk reduction.

S5_customer_disclosure.quote: When a model's thermal incident rate exceeds 8 incidents per 100,000 installed units in any 12-month period, the manufacturer must promptly notify the relevant regulator and provide incident records and a corrective-action proposal. ... Exceeding the threshold requires review but does not by itself mandate a recall. Regulators may also require a recall or equivalent protective action at lower rates where the evidence warrants it.

document.section_notes: The deal lands on the red-line-compatible side of S2 and S4 (per-model results go to buyers and regulators but are not published; suppression from 36 months with a regulator-approved equivalent), and on a 6-year retrofit deadline. It is weak where the companies had exposure: the 5% thermal-test threshold triggers only review with no sales stop, S5's 8/100k figure triggers only review and a corrective-action proposal with no automatic recall, and S1's reporting scope is limited to thermal runaway/fire/explosion/injury. S3's new-unit shut-off date of 3 years (vs the ≤12-month acceptable) is the clearest departure from the acceptable range, and S1/S5 customer-notice timings are strong.
